name: Coachix
subcategory: personal AI console with private knowledge and MCP tools
tagline: A personal AI assistant console that mixes private knowledge, MCP tools, reusable skills, and routing across models.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Every piece of this category is now commodity: chat UI, an embeddings table, an MCP client, a router that picks a model per request. An agent can hand you a working local console in one sitting, and the parts you actually touch daily, your own notes plus your own API keys, are the parts that port cleanly. The weekend goes to the unglamorous half: chunking that does not embarrass itself, MCP servers that crash and need restarting, per-tool permission prompts, and getting to it from your phone. Nothing here is defended by data or network, so the gap is maintenance and taste rather than access. If you enjoy owning the glue, own it; if you do not, the glue is exactly what a subscription buys.
coreLoopDIY: A local web console that chats over your own indexed notes, calls MCP tools with your approval, and routes each request to a cheap or strong model based on rules you set.
requirements: Node 20 and a local folder to run it in
At least two provider API keys so routing means something
A directory of your own documents to index
Willingness to restart a crashed MCP server yourself
whatYouLose: Access from a phone without you building auth and hosting first
A curated skills library, so every prompt template starts blank
A maintained connector list, so each new MCP server is your integration project
Retrieval quality someone else tuned; your first chunker will return the wrong paragraph
Someone absorbing provider API churn when a model is renamed or deprecated
moatNotes: Routing and retrieval are cheap to write and expensive to make consistently good; that gap is polish, not lock-in.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the assembly is easy and the upkeep is not. Model names change, providers rate-limit differently, MCP servers break in ways that look like your bug, and the defaults that make retrieval feel smart are dozens of small decisions you get to make wrong first. Paying here buys sane defaults, a tool catalog that mostly works, and access from a device other than the laptop where you built it. If you already live in a terminal and keep your own keys, that value shrinks fast.
notes: The chat-over-my-notes part is a single evening; the phone, the permissions, and the tool catalog are the rest of the weekend.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal AI assistant console. One user, my machine, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud services beyond the model providers themselves.

Stack, non-negotiable: TypeScript, Next.js App Router, SQLite via better-sqlite3 with the sqlite-vec extension for vectors, Tailwind for styling, the Vercel AI SDK for provider calls, and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk for MCP. No Docker, no Postgres, no auth library.

In scope:
1. Streaming chat UI with persistent conversations stored in SQLite. Sidebar of past threads, rename and delete.
2. Knowledge: a KNOWLEDGE_DIR env var pointing at a folder. An indexer script walks md, txt, and pdf files, chunks by heading then by roughly 800 tokens with overlap, embeds each chunk, and stores text plus vector plus source path and line range. Re-running the indexer updates changed files only, by mtime and hash.
3. Retrieval: top-k vector search injected into the system prompt, with visible citations under each answer that link to the source file and line range. Never cite a chunk that was not retrieved.
4. Model routing: a routing.json file with ordered rules matching on message length, presence of retrieved context, explicit slash commands, and a default. Each rule names a provider and model. Show the chosen model as a badge on every assistant message, and allow a manual override per thread.
5. Skills: markdown files in a skills folder, each with frontmatter for name, description, and optional model hint. Expose them in the composer as slash commands that prefill the prompt with argument substitution.
6. MCP: read mcp.json listing stdio servers with command and args. On boot, spawn them, list their tools, and expose the tools to the model. Every tool call must show a diff-style confirmation card with server name, tool name, and arguments, and wait for my approval unless the tool is in an allowlist. Log every call and result to SQLite. If a server dies, show it as offline and offer a restart button; do not crash the app.

Out of scope: user accounts, sharing, teams, mobile apps, billing, vector database services, and fine-tuning.

Secrets: all provider keys in .env.local, read server-side only, never exposed to the browser. Commit a .env.example.

Deliver a README with setup in under ten commands, a seed skills folder containing three examples, and one integration test that indexes a fixture folder and asserts that a query returns the expected chunk.
